items.stem: Which of the following best describes "significance level"?
options: Total frequency × probability of the category under H₀
(r − 1)(c − 1) for a table with r rows and c columns
The probability threshold (e.g. 5%) used to decide whether to reject H₀
Independent random samples from normally distributed populations (with equal variances for the pooled test)
items.answer: The probability threshold (e.g. 5%) used to decide whether to reject H₀
items.markingKey: C. "significance level" is the probability threshold (e.g. 5%) used to decide whether to reject H₀.

items.stem: "A p-value of 0.04 means there is a 4% chance that H₀ is true." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming H₀ is true, not the probability that H₀ is true.
items.markingKey: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming H₀ is true, not the probability that H₀ is true. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a study, a doctor investigates whether a drug changes mean systolic blood pressure from 120 mmHg. The test gives p = 0.0180. Mateo concludes: "H₁ is proven true." Explain why this conclusion is not appropriate and write a correct conclusion at the 10% level.
items.answer: reject H₀
items.markingKey: R1 hypothesis tests give evidence, not proof (there is a chance of a type I error); A1 0.0180 < 0.1; R1 there is significant evidence at the 10% level that the mean blood pressure ≠ 120.

items.stem: A student claims: "A p-value of 0.04 means there is a 4% chance that H₀ is true." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming H₀ is true, not the probability that H₀ is true.
items.markingKey: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming H₀ is true, not the probability that H₀ is true. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a study, a sports scientist believes a new training plan changes the mean 100 m time from 13 s. A t-test statistic of 3.11 (in the direction of H₁) is obtained with 8 degrees of freedom. Find the p-value and state the conclusion at the 1% level.
items.answer: p = 0.0144; do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: H₁: μ ≠ 13 ⇒ two-tailed (R1); p = 2 × P(T > 3.11) (M1) = 0.0144 (A1); compare with 0.01 (A1) do not reject H₀.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "A p-value of 0.04 means there is a 4% chance that H₀ is true." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming H₀ is true, not the probability that H₀ is true.
items.markingKey: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming H₀ is true, not the probability that H₀ is true. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Study 1 investigates whether the number of goals per match follows a Poisson distribution with mean 2.5. Study 2 investigates whether births are equally likely on each day of the week at a hospital. Study 3 investigates whether the colours of cars in a car park match national sales proportions. (a) For each study, name an appropriate test. (b) For each study, write the null hypothesis. (c) The p-values are 0.0780, 0.0330, 0.0810 respectively. State the conclusion of each at the 1% level. (d) Explain, for one study, what a type II error would mean. (e) Explain why a smaller significance level makes a type I error less likely.
items.answer: (a) χ² goodness of fit test; χ² goodness of fit test; χ² goodness of fit test (c) do not reject H₀; do not reject H₀; do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1 A1. (b) H₀: goals per match follow Po(2.5); H₀: births are uniformly distributed over the days; H₀: colours follow the national proportions (A1 A1 A1). (c) 0.0780 > 0.01; 0.0330 > 0.01; 0.0810 > 0.01 (A1 A1). (d) R1 failing to detect a real effect. (e) R1 H₀ is rejected only for more extreme results (P(type I error) = significance level).

items.stem: Study 1 investigates whether births are equally likely on each day of the week at a hospital. Study 2 investigates whether choice of school subject is associated with gender (survey counts). Study 3 investigates whether the proportion of left-handed people differs between three countries (counts of left/right-handed in each). (a) For each study, name an appropriate test. (b) For each study, write the null hypothesis. (c) The p-values are 0.0390, 0.125, 0.0590 respectively. State the conclusion of each at the 5% level. (d) Explain, for one study, what a type II error would mean. (e) Explain why a smaller significance level makes a type I error less likely.
items.answer: (a) χ² goodness of fit test; χ² test for independence; χ² test for independence (c) reject H₀; do not reject H₀; do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1 A1. (b) H₀: births are uniformly distributed over the days; H₀: subject choice and gender are independent; H₀: handedness and country are independent (A1 A1 A1). (c) 0.0390 < 0.05; 0.125 > 0.05; 0.0590 > 0.05 (A1 A1). (d) R1 failing to detect a real effect. (e) R1 H₀ is rejected only for more extreme results (P(type I error) = significance level).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "H₁, the statement accepted if H₀ is rejected; it may be one-tailed (<, >) or two-tailed (≠)"?
items.answer: alternative hypothesis
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of alternative hypothesis.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "null hypothesis".
items.answer: H₀, the default statement of no effect, no difference or independence, assumed true unless the evidence is strong
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: H₀, the default statement of no effect, no difference or independence, assumed true unless the evidence is strong. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why we say "do not reject H₀" rather than "accept H₀".
items.answer: A large p-value only shows that the data are consistent with H₀; it does not prove H₀ is true – the sample may be too small to detect a real effect.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A large p-value only shows that the data are consistent with H₀; it does not prove H₀ is true – the sample may be too small to detect a real effect. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In a study, a sports scientist believes a new training plan changes the mean 100 m time from 14 s. The test gives p = 0.0603. Freya concludes: "H₀ is proven true." Explain why this conclusion is not appropriate and write a correct conclusion at the 5% level.
items.answer: do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: R1 hypothesis tests give evidence, not proof (there is a chance of a type II error); A1 0.0603 > 0.05; R1 there is insufficient evidence at the 5% level to reject H₀.

items.stem: In a study, a factory says the mean mass of its cereal boxes is 750 g; a consumer group suspects under-filling. The test gives p = 0.0747. Noah concludes: "H₀ is proven true." Explain why this conclusion is not appropriate and write a correct conclusion at the 5% level.
items.answer: do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: R1 hypothesis tests give evidence, not proof (there is a chance of a type II error); A1 0.0747 > 0.05; R1 there is insufficient evidence at the 5% level to reject H₀.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a one-tailed and a two-tailed test.
items.answer: A one-tailed test looks for an effect in one specified direction (H₁: μ > μ₀ or μ < μ₀); a two-tailed test looks for any difference (H₁: μ ≠ μ₀), splitting the significance level between both tails.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A one-tailed test looks for an effect in one specified direction (H₁: μ > μ₀ or μ < μ₀); a two-tailed test looks for any difference (H₁: μ ≠ μ₀), splitting the significance level between both tails. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In a study, a doctor investigates whether a drug changes mean systolic blood pressure from 125 mmHg. A t-test statistic of 1.47 (in the direction of H₁) is obtained with 18 degrees of freedom. Find the p-value and state the conclusion at the 1% level.
items.answer: p = 0.159; do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: H₁: μ ≠ 125 ⇒ two-tailed (R1); p = 2 × P(T > 1.47) (M1) = 0.159 (A1); compare with 0.01 (A1) do not reject H₀.

items.stem: In a study, a doctor investigates whether a drug changes mean systolic blood pressure from 125 mmHg. A t-test statistic of 2.8 (in the direction of H₁) is obtained with 16 degrees of freedom. Find the p-value and state the conclusion at the 10% level.
items.answer: p = 0.0128; reject H₀
items.markingKey: H₁: μ ≠ 125 ⇒ two-tailed (R1); p = 2 × P(T > 2.8) (M1) = 0.0128 (A1); compare with 0.1 (A1) reject H₀.

items.stem: In a study, a factory says the mean mass of its cereal boxes is 1000 g; a consumer group suspects under-filling. A t-test statistic of 2.9 (in the direction of H₁) is obtained with 13 degrees of freedom. Find the p-value and state the conclusion at the 10% level.
items.answer: p = 0.00620; reject H₀
items.markingKey: H₁: μ < 1000 ⇒ one-tailed (R1); p = P(T > 2.9) (M1) = 0.00620 (A1); compare with 0.1 (A1) reject H₀.

items.stem: In a study, a teacher believes a revision app raises the mean test score above 60%. A t-test statistic of 2.89 (in the direction of H₁) is obtained with 16 degrees of freedom. Find the p-value and state the conclusion at the 1% level.
items.answer: p = 0.00533; reject H₀
items.markingKey: H₁: μ > 60 ⇒ one-tailed (R1); p = P(T > 2.89) (M1) = 0.00533 (A1); compare with 0.01 (A1) reject H₀.

items.stem: Study 1 investigates whether the proportion of left-handed people differs between three countries (counts of left/right-handed in each). Study 2 investigates whether the colours of cars in a car park match national sales proportions. Study 3 investigates whether a spinner with five sectors is fair, from 200 spins. (a) For each study, name an appropriate test. (b) For each study, write the null hypothesis. (c) The p-values are 0.0750, 0.0260, 0.147 respectively. State the conclusion of each at the 5% level. (d) Explain, for one study, what a type II error would mean. (e) Explain why a smaller significance level makes a type I error less likely.
items.answer: (a) χ² test for independence; χ² goodness of fit test; χ² goodness of fit test (c) do not reject H₀; reject H₀; do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1 A1. (b) H₀: handedness and country are independent; H₀: colours follow the national proportions; H₀: each sector is equally likely (A1 A1 A1). (c) 0.0750 > 0.05; 0.0260 < 0.05; 0.147 > 0.05 (A1 A1). (d) R1 failing to detect a real effect. (e) R1 H₀ is rejected only for more extreme results (P(type I error) = significance level).

items.stem: Study 1 investigates whether births are equally likely on each day of the week at a hospital. Study 2 investigates whether boys and girls in a class have different mean reaction times. Study 3 investigates whether the mean commuting time differs between cyclists and bus users (two small samples of times). (a) For each study, name an appropriate test. (b) For each study, write the null hypothesis. (c) The p-values are 0.113, 0.0780, 0.0950 respectively. State the conclusion of each at the 1% level. (d) Explain, for one study, what a type II error would mean. (e) Explain why a smaller significance level makes a type I error less likely.
items.answer: (a) χ² goodness of fit test; two-sample t-test; two-sample t-test (c) do not reject H₀; do not reject H₀; do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1 A1. (b) H₀: births are uniformly distributed over the days; H₀: μ_boys = μ_girls; H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ (A1 A1 A1). (c) 0.113 > 0.01; 0.0780 > 0.01; 0.0950 > 0.01 (A1 A1). (d) R1 failing to detect a real effect. (e) R1 H₀ is rejected only for more extreme results (P(type I error) = significance level).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "expected frequency".
items.answer: (row total × column total)/grand total, the frequency expected if the variables are independent
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: (row total × column total)/grand total, the frequency expected if the variables are independent. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Rejecting H₀ in a χ² test proves that one variable causes the other." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It only shows evidence of an association; causation needs further reasoning or an experiment.
items.markingKey: It only shows evidence of an association; causation needs further reasoning or an experiment. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the χ² test for independence is always one-tailed (upper tail).
items.answer: Any departure from independence makes (O − E)² larger, so only large values of χ² provide evidence against H₀. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Any departure from independence makes (O − E)² larger, so only large values of χ² provide evidence against H₀. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A large χ² statistic suggests…

items.answer: the observed frequencies differ greatly from those expected under independence

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A two-way table of observed frequencies for two categorical variables"?

items.stem: Explain why categories may need to be combined in a χ² test.
items.answer: If some expected frequencies are below 5 the χ² distribution is a poor approximation; combining adjacent categories increases the expected values (and reduces the degrees of freedom).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If some expected frequencies are below 5 the χ² distribution is a poor approximation; combining adjacent categories increases the expected values (and reduces the degrees of freedom). items.stem: A public-health study records gender against opinion on a new park: male: agree 27, neutral 50, disagree 25; female: agree 20, neutral 36, disagree 18. A χ² test gives p = 0.997. items.answer: do not reject H₀
items.markingKey: A1 0.997 > 0.01, so do not reject H₀; R1 insufficient evidence of an association; R1 association is not causation (other factors may be involved; the study is observational).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "expected frequency (goodness of fit)"?
options: A test of whether observed frequencies fit a proposed distribution, using χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E
Total frequency × probability of the category under H₀
A test comparing the means of two independent samples when population standard deviations are unknown
A test of H₀: the two variables are independent, using χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E
items.answer: Total frequency × probability of the category under H₀
items.markingKey: B. "expected frequency (goodness of fit)" is total frequency × probability of the category under H₀.

items.stem: A student claims: "A χ² goodness of fit test can use percentages instead of frequencies." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The test must use actual frequencies (counts); using percentages changes the χ² value and the conclusion.
items.markingKey: The test must use actual frequencies (counts); using percentages changes the χ² value and the conclusion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A six-sided die is rolled 80 times: 1 10, 2 15, 3 15, 4 13, 5 13, 6 14. To test whether the die is fair, Mateo calculates χ² using the percentages of each category instead of the frequencies. Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: χ² must use frequencies
items.markingKey: R1 χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E depends on the sample size; R1 using percentages pretends the sample size is 100, changing the statistic (here χ² = 1.30 with n = 80); A1 the conclusion could change.
